title: Epochal fairness and kernel-steering experiments
content:
Summary

This note documents an experimental design and early results for an epochal (epoch-based) fairness coordinator that steers kernel selection and batching behavior. The goal: reconcile token-level efficiency (high GPU utilization and low per-token cost) with request-level latency SLOs and per-customer fairness. This is a working doc — sketches, rough numbers, and TODOs are interleaved.

Motivation

We have two recurring conflicts in production:
- Kernel-level batching/packets that maximize throughput occasionally starve small interactive requests (p95 latency regressions).
- Per-customer burstiness (lots of short chats) ends up dominated by long streaming requests from other tenants because batching groups by kernel-friendly sequences.

Existing approaches (continuous token-level batching) are fast on aggregate but opaque for SLAs. We want an explicit coordinator that reasons in discrete epochs (windows) about fairness and also nudges kernel choices (quantized kernels, FP16 vs int8 execution paths) to reduce variance.

High-level idea

1) Epochs: time is divided into short epochs (e.g., 10–50ms). During each epoch the coordinator: collects in-flight requests, computes fair token budget allocations per tenant/route, and produces a set of microbatches (each ties to a chosen kernel variant).
2) Kernel steering: for each microbatch we attach a kernel hint (fast-low-precision, balanced, high-quality) determined via a cost-latency-utility function. The coordinator can bias packing to prefer kernels that preserve latency for high-priority tenants.
3) Aging and credits: tenants accumulate fairness credits when they receive less than their proportional share; credits decay on a configurable timescale. Credits can be spent to get earlier scheduling or a higher-quality kernel.

Objectives and constraints

- Primary: preserve interactive p95/p99 latency targets for routes marked latency-sensitive.
- Secondary: maximize tokens/sec on GPUs and minimize average cost-per-token.
- Soft constraint: avoid excessive kernel switching that increases kernel init overhead or occupancy churn.
- Practical: keep epoch scheduling CPU overhead low (< 1% of host CPU at 1000 req/s).

Coordinator components (sketch)

A. Ingress queue sampler
- Lightweight sampler tags incoming requests with tenant_id, route, priority, estimated token_count.
- Short requests (< 8 tokens expected) are flagged as micro-interactive.

B. Epoch collector
- On epoch boundary (configurable wall-clock or adaptive based on arrival rate), collector snapshots the queue and groups candidates.
- Compute demand per tenant: sum of requested tokens for requests that arrived in epoch.

C. Fairness allocator
- Inputs: tenant demand, tenant weight (configurable), stored credits, latency-service tier (SLO flags).
- Output: token_budget per tenant for this epoch.
- Simple allocation rule (prototype): budget_t = clamp((weight_t / sum_weights) * epoch_capacity + credits_t, 0, max_token_window)
- Credits update: credits_t += (nominal_share - actual_served) * alpha; decay credits *= decay_factor per epoch.

D. Microbatch assembler with kernel hints
- For each tenant budget, assemble microbatches trying to pack similarly-lengthed KV cache affinities.
- Kernel hint selection: score_k = w_cost * cost_k + w_lat * predicted_latency_k - w_qual * quality_drop_k - w_switch * switching_penalty (if previous kernel != k). Choose k with min score subject to tenant's latency tier.

E. Deadline queue and preemption policy
- Microbatches inherit deadlines from the earliest request they contain. If a microbatch misses a deadline window and a higher-priority microbatch arrives, coordinator can preempt by creating a tiny prioritized microbatch (preemption granularity is request-level).

Token-level vs request-level tension (note to self)

- Token-level packing maximizes throughput (you can fill GPU with lots of tokens from many requests). But it's harder to measure/guarantee request-level latency (a request waiting for tokens may be split across microbatches).
- Request-level fairness treats each request atomically (serve whole request earlier) but loses utilization when requests are small and misaligned by length.

Proposal compromise:
- Maintain two lanes per epoch: interactive lane (request-level, small requests prioritized), throughput lane (token-level packing for large/background requests). The allocator splits epoch capacity across lanes (configurable ratio, dynamically adjustable based on SLO violations).

Kernel-steering specifics

- Kernel variants: fast_int8, balanced_fp16, high_quality_bf16. Each has different per-token latency and quality penalty (measured via eval hooks).
- Maintain a small running model of per-variant latency given current occupancy and sequence-length distribution. Use exponential moving averages.
- Steering policy: for tenants in latency-sensitive tier, bias towards balanced_fp16 unless credits say otherwise; for background tenants bias towards fast_int8.

Pseudocode (very rough)

on_epoch_boundary():
  snapshot = drain_sampler_window()
  demand = compute_demand(snapshot)
  budgets = fairness_allocator(demand, weights, credits)
  lanes = split_into_lanes(snapshot, budgets)
  microbatches = []
  for lane in lanes:
    while lane.has_unserved():
      mb = pack_next_microbatch(lane, target_tokens=epoch_slice_tokens)
      mb.kernel = pick_kernel_hint(mb, tenant_priority, prev_kernel)
      microbatches.append(mb)
  schedule_microbatches(microbatches)

Preliminary experiments (instrumentation notes + numbers are rough)

- Testbed: 1xA100, synthetic mixed workload: 60% short chats (2–10 tokens), 30% medium (20–60 tokens), 10% long (200+ tokens).
- Baselines: continuous token-batcher (current), request-priority scheduler (strict request atomic).

Results (pilot run, 5m window):
- Baseline continuous: avg tokens/sec 62k, p95 latency (interactive route) = 210ms, p99 = 780ms
- Request-priority: avg tokens/sec 48k, p95 = 120ms, p99 = 340ms
- Epochal-coordinator (epoch=25ms, lanes split 30/70 interactive/throughput, kernel steering enabled): avg tokens/sec 58k, p95 = 130ms, p99 = 360ms

Observations:
- Epochal approach achieves much of the latency benefit of request-priority while recouping most throughput of token-level batching.
- Kernel steering reduced p99 for long background requests because it avoided kernel switches mid-sequence.

Cost of coordination

- CPU overhead measured: ~0.6% host CPU at 800 rps for prototype implementation in Go (single-threaded epoch loop).
- Memory: extra metadata per request ~ 120 bytes for credits, tenant pointers, kernel_hint.

Open questions and risks

- Kernel switch cost under real multi-tenant loads: switching penalty modeled but needs real trace evaluation.
- Do credits introduce starvation risk if a tenant consistently overspends? Need max_credit cap and backpressure to client.
- Interaction with KV cache affinity: packing by token length is cheap, but preserving KV cache locality matters for long chat continuations — need affinity-aware packer.
- Adaptive epoch sizing: fixed vs dynamic epoch boundary tradeoffs (latency vs batching efficiency).

Immediate next steps (short-term experiments)

- Implement affinity-aware packer stub in the runtime (PR link above).
- Run multi-tenant replay with real logs (SERV-1023) and measure kernel-switch rates.
- Tune lane split controller that bumps interactive lane if p95 > target for > 10 epochs.

TODOs / notes to self

- Add jitter to epoch boundary to avoid pathological arrival alignment.
- Add operator controls on credit decay and max_credit per tenant.
- Evaluate with dedicated GPU pools and with autoscaling enabled (does epoch length need to be scaled?).
- Bring this design to arch review once the affinity packer prototype lands.

Appendix: quick FAQ

Q: Why epochs and not continuous token-streaming?
A: Epochs make fairness explicit and allow us to reason about per-epoch budgets and kernel choices. Continuous streaming is efficient but opaque; we need an explicit control plane for SLOs.

Q: Will this increase tail variance?
A: It can if epochs misalign or credits are poorly tuned. Early experiments show better p95/p99 for interactive tenants, but more testing required for mixed long-sequence workloads.

Q: Can this be layered on Dedicated pools?
A: Yes — in Dedicated we can set different weights and longer epochs (higher throughput) if customers accept higher median latency.

End of draft.

(If you're reading this: leave comments inline; this is intentionally a thin spec to stimulate prototypes.)
